CHAPTER IX.

HIGH AND LOW.


At the foot of the stairs, Mr. Gryce excused himself, and calling in two
or three men whom he had left outside, had the valet removed before
taking Miss Butterworth back into the study. When all was quiet again,
and they found an opportunity to speak, Mr. Gryce remarked:

"One very important thing has been settled by the experiment we have
just made. Bartow is acquitted of participation in this crime."

"Then we can give our full attention to the young people. You have heard
nothing from them, I suppose?"

"No."

"Nor from the old man who laughed?"

"No."

Miss Butterworth looked disappointed.

"I thought--it seemed very probable--that the scrap of writing you found
would inform you who these were. If it was important enough for the
dying man to try to swallow it, it certainly should give some clew to
his assailant."

"Unfortunately, it does not do so. It was a veritable scrawl, madam,
running something like this: 'I return your daughter to you. She is
here. Neither she nor you will ever see me again. Remember Evelyn!' And
signed, 'Amos's son.'"

"Amos's son! That is Mr. Adams himself."

"So we have every reason to believe."

"Strange! Unaccountable! And the paper inscribed with these words was
found clinched between his teeth! Was the handwriting recognized?"

"Yes, as his own, if we can judge from the specimens we have seen of his
signature on the fly-leaves of his books."

"Well, mysteries deepen. And the retaining of this paper was so
important to him that even in his death throe he thrust it in this
strangest of all hiding-places, as being the only one that could be
considered safe from search. And the girl! Her first words on coming to
herself were: 'You have left that line of writing behind.' Mr. Gryce,
those words, few and inexplicable as they are, contain the key to the
whole situation. Will you repeat them again, if you please, sentence by
sentence?"

"With pleasure, madam; I have said them often enough to myself. First,
then: 'I return your daughter to you!'"

"So! Mr. Adams had some one's daughter in charge whom he returns. Whose
daughter? Not that young man's daughter, certainly, for that would
necessitate her being a small child. Besides, if these words had been
meant for his assailant, why make so remarkable an effort to hide them
from him?"

"Very true! I have said the same thing to myself."

"Yet, if not for him, for whom, then? For the old gentleman who came in
later?"

"It is possible; since hearing of him I have allowed myself to regard
this as among the possibilities, especially as the next words of this
strange communication are: 'She is here.' Now the only woman who was
there a few minutes previous to this old gentleman's visit was the
light-haired girl whom you saw carried out."

"Very true; but why do you reason as if this paper had just been
written? It might have been an old scrap, referring to past sorrows or
secrets."

"These words were written that afternoon. The paper on which they were
scrawled was torn from a sheet of letter paper lying on the desk, and
the pen with which they were inscribed--you must have noticed where it
lay, quite out of its natural place on the extreme edge of the table."

"Certainly, sir; but I had little idea of the significance we might come
to attach to it. These words are connected, then, with the girl I saw.
And she is not Evelyn or he would not have repeated in this note the
bird's catch-word, 'Remember Evelyn!' I wonder if she is Evelyn?"
proceeded Miss Butterworth, pointing to the one large picture which
adorned the wall.

"We may call her so for the nonce. So melancholy a face may well suggest
some painful family secret. But how explain the violent part played by
the young man, who is not mentioned in these abrupt and hastily penned
sentences! It is all a mystery, madam, a mystery which we are wasting
time to attempt to solve."

"Yet I hate to give it up without an effort. Those words, now. There
were some other words you have not repeated to me."

"They came before that injunction, 'Remember Evelyn!' They bespoke a
resolve. 'Neither she nor you will ever see me again.'"

"Ah! but these few words are very significant, Mr. Gryce. Could he have
dealt that blow himself? May he have been a suicide after all?"

"Madam, you have the right to inquire; but from Bartow's pantomime, you
must have perceived it is not a self-inflicted blow he mimics, but a
maddened thrust from an outraged hand. Let us keep to our first
conclusions; only--to be fair to every possibility--the condition of Mr.
Adams's affairs and the absence of all family papers and such documents
as may usually be found in a wealthy man's desk prove that he had made
some preparation for possible death. It may have come sooner than he
expected and in another way, but it was a thought he had indulged in,
and--madam, I have a confession to make also. I have not been quite fair
to my most valued colleague. The study--that most remarkable of
rooms--contains a secret which has not been imparted to you; a very
peculiar one, madam, which was revealed to me in a rather startling
manner. This room can be, or rather could be, cut off entirely from the
rest of the house; made a death-trap of, or rather a tomb, in which this
incomprehensible man may have intended to die. Look at this plate of
steel. It is worked by a mechanism which forces it across this open
doorway. I was behind that plate of steel the other night, and these
holes had to be made to let me out."

"Ha! You detectives have your experiences! I should not have enjoyed
spending that especial evening with you. But what an old-world tragedy
we are unearthing here! I declare"--and the good lady actually rubbed
her eyes--"I feel as if transported back to mediæval days. Who says we
are living in New York within sound of the cable car and the singing of
the telegraph wire?"

"Some men are perfectly capable of bringing the mediæval into Wall
Street. I think Mr. Adams was one of those men. Romanticism tinged all
his acts, even the death he died. Nor did it cease with his death. It
followed him to the tomb. Witness the cross we found lying on his
bosom."

"That was the act of another's hand, the result of another's
superstition. That shows the presence of a priest or a woman at the
moment he died."

"Yet," proceeded Mr. Gryce, with a somewhat wondering air, "he must have
had a grain of hard sense in his make-up. All his contrivances worked.
He was a mechanical genius, as well as a lover of mystery."

"An odd combination. Strange that we do not feel his spirit infecting
the very air of this study. I could almost wish it did. We might then be
led to grasp the key to this mystery."

"That," remarked Mr. Gryce, "can be done in only one way. You have
already pointed it out. We must trace the young couple who were present
at his death struggle. If they cannot be found the case is hopeless."

"And so," said she, "we come around to the point from which we
started--proof positive that we are lost in the woods." And Miss
Butterworth rose. She felt that for the time being she, at least, had
come to the end of her resources.

Mr. Gryce did not seek to detain her. Indeed, he appeared to be anxious
to leave the place himself. They, however, stopped long enough to cast
one final look around them. As they did so Miss Butterworth's finger
slowly rose.

"See!" said she, "you can hardly perceive from this side of the wall the
opening made by the removal of that picture on the stair landing.
Wouldn't you say that it was in the midst of those folds of dark-colored
tapestry up there?"

"Yes, I had already located that spot as the one. With the picture hung
up on the other side, it would be quite invisible."

"One needs to keep one's eyes moving in a case like this. That picture
must have been drawn aside several times while we were in this room. Yet
we failed to notice it."

"That was from not looking high enough. High and low, Mr. Gryce! What
goes on at the level of the eye is apparent to every one."

The smile with which he acknowledged this parting shot and prepared to
escort her to the door had less of irony than sadness in it. Was he
beginning to realize that years tell even on the most sagacious, and
that neither high places nor low would have escaped his attention a
dozen years before?

Once the room fell silent once more, allowing them a private moment to converse, Mr. Gryce began.

"One crucial matter has been resolved by the experiment we just conducted," he stated. "Bartow is cleared of any involvement in this crime."

Miss Butterworth nodded, though her expression remained somber. "Then we may devote our full attention to the young people. Have you received anything from them?"

"No," Gryce replied. "Nor from the elderly man who arrived shortly afterward."

A shadow of disappointment crossed Miss Butterworth's face. "I had hoped—indeed, it seemed highly probable—that the fragment of writing you discovered would identify these individuals. If it was vital enough for a dying man to attempt swallowing, surely it must hold a clue to his attacker."

"Regrettably, it offers no such lead, madam," Gryce explained gently. "It was merely a hurried scrawl, reading something like this: *'I return your daughter to you. She is here. Neither she nor you will ever see me again. Remember Evelyn!'* Signed simply, *'Amos's son.'*"

"'Amos's son!' That is Mr. Adams himself," she observed.

"Precisely. We have ample reason to believe it is him."

"Extraordinary! Inexplicable! And yet, this paper was found clamped tightly between his teeth! Was the handwriting verified?"

"Yes," Gryce confirmed. "It matches his known signatures found on the fly-leaves of his books."

"Well, the mysteries only deepen," Miss Butterworth murmured. "The fact that he retained this note until his final throes suggests it was the only hiding place he deemed secure from search. And the girl! Upon regaining consciousness, her first words were: *'You have left that line of writing behind.'* Mr. Gryce, those words—few and enigmatic as they are—hold the key to the entire situation. Would you kindly repeat them to me, sentence by sentence?"

"With great pleasure, madam; I have recited them to myself countless times. First: *'I return your daughter to you!'"*

"So," Miss Butterworth analyzed, pacing slightly. "Mr. Adams had someone else's daughter in his care whom he is returning. Whose daughter? Certainly not that young man's, for that would imply she is a small child. Furthermore, if these words were intended for his assailant, why conceal them so meticulously?"

"I have pondered exactly that," Gryce admitted.

"Yet, if not for him, then for whom? Perhaps for the elderly gentleman who entered moments later?"

"It is a distinct possibility," Gryce conceded. "Since learning of his arrival, I have considered this scenario, particularly given the subsequent phrase: *'She is here.'* The only woman present immediately prior to the old man's entrance was the light-haired girl you witnessed being carried out."

"That is logical," Miss Butterworth agreed. "But why treat this document as if it were just written? It could easily be an old scrap referencing past sorrows or secrets."

"These words were composed that very afternoon," Gryce corrected firmly. "The paper was torn from a sheet resting on the desk, and the pen used to write them lay quite out of place on the extreme edge of the table."

"Certainly, sir; but I had not grasped the significance we might attribute to such details. Thus, these words concern the girl I saw. And she is not Evelyn, for otherwise, he would not have invoked the bird's catchphrase, *'Remember Evelyn!'* Do you wonder if she is Evelyn?" she asked, gesturing toward the single large portrait adorning the wall.

"We may provisionally assume she is," Gryce suggested. "Such a melancholy visage naturally hints at some painful family secret. However, how do we account for the violent role played by the young man, who remains unmentioned in these abrupt, hastily penned lines? It is a riddle, madam, and one we seem to be wasting precious time attempting to solve."

"Yet, I detest surrendering without making an earnest effort," Miss Butterworth insisted. "There were other words you omitted from your repetition."

"They preceded the command, *'Remember Evelyn!'* They spoke of a resolve: *'Neither she nor you will ever see me again.'"*

"Ah!" Miss Butterworth exclaimed. "Those few words are profoundly significant, Mr. Gryce. Could he have struck that blow himself? Might this have been a suicide after all?"

"Madam, you are entitled to ask; however, based on Bartow's pantomime, you must have deduced that the wound mimicked a maddened thrust from an enraged hand, not a self-inflicted strike. Let us adhere to our initial conclusion. Nevertheless—to ensure fairness to every possibility—the chaotic state of Mr. Adams's affairs and the conspicuous absence of family papers or standard documents typically found in a wealthy man's desk indicate he had prepared for a potential demise. It may have occurred sooner than anticipated, or in a different manner, but it was a thought he had entertained. Moreover, I must confess a lapse in my own judgment regarding my most valued colleague. The study—that most remarkable chamber—harbors a secret never shared with you. A peculiar revelation, madam, disclosed to me in a startling fashion. This room can be, or rather, could be, completely isolated from the rest of the house; transformed into a death trap, or indeed, a tomb wherein this incomprehensible man may have intended to pass away. Observe this steel plate. It operates via a mechanism designed to slide across this open doorway. Last night, I stood behind that plate, and these holes were forced through specifically to allow my escape."

"Hah! Detectives have their own trials!" Miss Butterworth laughed nervously, rubbing her eyes. "I should not have relished spending that particular evening with you. But what an archaic tragedy we are uncovering here! I declare—I feel as if transported back to medieval times. Who claims we live in New York, within earshot of cable cars and the chirping of telegraph wires?"

"Some men possess the unique ability to bring the medieval era to Wall Street," Gryce replied with a wry smile. "I believe Mr. Adams was one of those men. Romanticism permeated every aspect of his life, even the manner of his death. Nor did it cease with his passing; it followed him to the grave. Consider the cross we discovered lying upon his chest."

"That was the work of another's hand, born of another's superstition. It indicates the presence of a priest or a woman at the moment of his death."

"And yet," Gryce continued, his tone shifting to one of mild wonder, "he must have possessed a measure of hard sense within his constitution. Every contrivance functioned correctly. He was a mechanical genius as much as a lover of mystery."

"A strange amalgamation. It is curious that we do not feel his spirit infecting the very air of this study. One could almost wish it did; perhaps then we might grasp the solution to this puzzle."

"That," Gryce noted, "can be achieved in only one way. You have already indicated the path. We must track down the young couple who were present during his final struggle. If they cannot be found, the case is hopeless."

"And so," Miss Butterworth sighed, "we circle back to the starting point—a definitive proof that we are hopelessly lost in the woods." She rose abruptly. She felt that, for the moment, her own resources had reached their limit. Mr. Gryce made no move to detain her; indeed, he appeared eager to depart the premises himself. Nevertheless, they paused long enough to cast one final glance around the room. As they did so, Miss Butterworth's finger slowly rose.

"Look!" she whispered. "From this angle of the wall, you can barely discern the opening created by removing that picture on the stair landing. Would you not say it lies amidst those folds of dark tapestry up there?"

"Yes," Gryce replied, nodding. "I had already pinpointed that exact location. With the picture hung on the opposite side, it would remain entirely invisible."

"One must keep one's eyes moving in a case like this," she declared triumphantly. "That picture must have been shifted aside several times while we occupied this room, yet we failed to notice. That was because we were not looking high enough. High and low, Mr. Gryce! What occurs at the level of the eye is obvious to everyone."

The smile with which he acknowledged this parting observation and prepared to escort her to the door held less irony than a touch of sadness.
